turns.prompt_text: I'd like to relearn UML, but I don't know about how to go about doing so
turns.response_html:
Instead of trying to memorize all 14 official diagram types, the most efficient way to get back up to speed is to treat UML as a practical whiteboarding language rather than a strict dogma. For modern software architecture—especially when designing multi-agent execution loops or mapping out complex state changes—you really only need to master a few key concepts.

1. Focus on the "Big Three"

Most engineering teams rely on just three core diagrams to communicate complex logic and structure:

  • Class Diagrams (Structure): The backbone of object-oriented and data-driven design. These map out your structs/classes, methods, and how different components inherit from, compose, or depend on each other.
  • Sequence Diagrams (Behavior): Essential for mapping out execution loops and asynchronous processes. They show how different actors, services, or internal modules interact over time, step-by-step.
  • State Machine Diagrams (Logic): Perfect for tracking the lifecycle of a complex entity as it shifts between different states based on specific triggers.

2. Ditch the GUI for Diagram-as-Code

Instead of dragging and dropping boxes in a heavy GUI, use text-based diagramming tools. They integrate seamlessly into version control and markdown-based knowledge graphs built on local text files.

  • Mermaid.js: Incredibly popular, lightweight, and renders natively in GitHub, Notion, and Obsidian.
  • PlantUML: A highly robust, text-based tool perfect for highly detailed, complex architectural maps.

3. Learn by Reverse-Engineering

The fastest way to relearn the syntax is to apply it to a codebase you already know intimately. Take a recent local utility or a Rust project and work backward:

  1. Map the core data structures and traits into a Class Diagram.
  2. Take the primary execution loop and map the function calls into a Sequence Diagram.
  3. Compare your sketches against standard UML documentation to refine the specifics: arrow types (solid vs. dashed), multiplicity (e.g., 1..*), and access modifiers (+, -, #).

4. High-Yield Resources

  • "UML Distilled" by Martin Fowler: The gold standard for developers. It focuses purely on what is practically useful in the real world and skips the academic bloat.
  • Refactoring.guru: Offers fantastic, visually clear explanations of software design patterns alongside their accompanying UML diagrams, making it easy to connect the code to the model.
